==Problem==

Which of the following expressions is never a prime number when <math>p</math> is a prime number?

<math>\textbf{(A) } p^2+16 \qquad \textbf{(B) } p^2+24 \qquad \textbf{(C) } p^2+26 \qquad \textbf{(D) } p^2+46 \qquad \textbf{(E) } p^2+96</math>

=Solutions=

==Solution 1==
Each expression is in the form <imath>p^2 + n</imath>.

All prime numbers are of the form <imath>6k \pm 1</imath>, AKA they are congruent to <imath>\pm1 \pmod{6}</imath>. We can utilize this nicely to check for what we are looking for. If the expression is a prime, then


<imath>p^2 + n \equiv \pm1 \pmod{6}</imath>

<imath>\Rightarrow (\pm1)^2 + n \equiv \pm1 \pmod{6}</imath>

<imath>\Rightarrow 1 + n \equiv \pm1 \pmod{6}</imath>

<imath>\Rightarrow n \equiv (\pm1) - 1 \pmod{6}</imath>

<imath>\Rightarrow n \equiv (1</imath> <imath>or</imath> <imath>-1) - 1 \pmod{6}</imath>

<imath>\Rightarrow n \equiv 0</imath> <imath>or</imath> <imath>-2 \pmod{6}</imath>


Now, just check for <imath>n</imath> in each option using this condition to check whether its prime or not.

<cmath>(A)\ n = 16; prime</cmath>
<cmath>(B)\ n = 24; prime</cmath>
<cmath>(C)\ n = 26; not\ prime</cmath>
<cmath>(D)\ n = 46; prime</cmath>
<cmath>(E)\ n = 96; prime</cmath>

Therefore, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } p^2 + 26} </imath>.

~ <imath>shalomkeshet</imath>


==Solution 2==

Because squares of a non-multiple of 3 is always <imath>1 \pmod{3}</imath>, the only expression always a multiple of <imath>3</imath> is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } p^2+26} </imath>. This is excluding when <imath>p\equiv 0 \pmod{3}</imath>, which only occurs when <imath>p=3</imath>, then <imath>p^2+26=35</imath> which is still composite.

==Solution 3==

\( p^2 + 16 \) is prime for \( p = 5 \), so we know that \( A \) doesn't work.

Because \( p^2 + 96 = p^2 + (16) \cdot 6 \), we see that eventually there exists a number \( p \) that makes the sum prime, therefore \( E \) also doesn't work.

Option \( B \) is \( p^2 + 24 \), but because the number itself has no carryover, we can assume \( p = 5 \) again to get the number \( 41 \), which is prime.

Option \( D \) is \( p^2 + 46 \), ending in \( 6 \), so we try \( p = 5 \) again to get \( 71 \). This is also prime.

We can either deduce through elimination that \( p^2 + 26 \) is always composite for any prime \( p \), but we can prove it by showing \( p = 5 \) doesn't work, \( p = 7 \) doesn't work, and \( p = 11 \) doesn't work, and through [https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/Induction?srsltid=AfmBOooY-SKw1NAbaPWjFKkyfSoHj6RXiwWuqty6FtGzCI5GAw7eyCTA Engineer's Induction], \( p^2 + 26 \) always remains composite.

Therefore the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } p^2 + 26} </imath>.

~Pinotation

==Solution 4 (Answer Choices)==

Since the question asks which of the following will never be a prime number when <imath>p</imath> is a prime number, a way to find the answer is by trying to find a value for <imath>p</imath> such that the statement above won't be true.

A) <imath>p^2+16</imath> isn't true when <imath>p=5</imath> because <imath>25+16=41</imath>, which is prime

B) <imath>p^2+24</imath> isn't true when <imath>p=7</imath> because <imath>49+24=73</imath>, which is prime

C) <imath>p^2+26</imath>

D) <imath>p^2+46</imath> isn't true when <imath>p=5</imath> because <imath>25+46=71</imath>, which is prime

E) <imath>p^2+96</imath> isn't true when <imath>p=19</imath> because <imath>361+96=457</imath>, which is prime

Therefore, <imath>\framebox{C}</imath> is the correct answer.

-DAWAE
